transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-02
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Rodriguez (Redwood SE), Priya Malhotra (BlueHarbor), Tomás Ortega (BlueHarbor CTO), Lena Brooks (BlueHarbor Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated):
- Goal: Scope a 3-week POC around input sanitization, logging/redaction, retention settings, and a mini throughput/latency benchmark.
- Success criteria discussed: P95 latency target, redaction / zero-storage option, encryption + KMS, and a reproducible benchmark harness.
- Next steps: SOW, benchmark harness, sample prompt corpus, follow-up benchmark run.

Topics raised: success criteria, workload sizing, data handling (PII/PHI), prompt storage, retention TTLs, KMS/HSM, routing hosted vs dedicated, mini-benchmark plan, timeline/sprint plan.

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, this is Avery from Redwood, and with me is Marcus our solutions engineer. We're hoping to scope the POC so we can give you a clear test plan, success criteria, and the data handling guardrails.
[00:12] Tomás: Hey, thanks. Quick note on timing — we've got an internal board review on 3/25 so ideally POC wrap by 3/20, is that doable?
[00:22] Marcus: Uh yeah, we can do a condensed sprint, we usually run a 2–3 week POC with a mini benchmark first week, then remediation, then longer soak. We can adapt.
[00:30] Priya: Good. Main concerns from infra side: we cannot leak raw PII to a public hosted endpoint except for redacted tokens. We need either VPC/private deployment or a guarantee of no prompt persistence.
[00:41] Avery: Totally. For this POC we can offer two modes: hosted with no persistent prompt storage (ephemeral only) or dedicated/private with customer-managed KMS and optional on-prem. Which do you prefer for the trial?
[00:52] Lena: Security says we want KMS integration and audit logs. If hosted, we need proof that prompts are not written to disk and that KMS keys are customer-owned.
[01:02] Marcus: Understood. We have a Customer KMS option for Dedicated or Private. For hosted we can enable a no-retention flag that prevents prompt persistence in analytics and disables long-term prompt storage - but there is a config flag and we can provide attestations plus audit streaming.
[01:15] Priya: What does "no-retention flag" actually mean? Do you still keep logs for debugging for 7 days? What about telemetry?
[01:23] Avery: Good question. When no-retention is on, by default we only keep ephemeral traces for the duration of the request for debugging: 24–72 hours configurable, or zero-retention which drops everything immediately aside from minimal audit events required for billing. We can also redact or hash tokens before any logs leave the runtime.
[01:39] Tomás: Hashing is ok if it's irreversible, but we still need a way to link an incident back to the request id; we need pseudonymous IDs but not the raw prompt.
[01:49] Marcus: Yep, we typically provide a request id plus a salted hash of the prompt portion. Salt is customer-specific under KMS in Dedicated mode.
[01:58] Lena: And what about PII detection? Do you do automatic redaction? Or do we run a pre-pass?
[02:05] Marcus: We have an optional preprocessor that can remove obvious PII patterns (credit card, ssn, email), but it's heuristic — for robust protection we recommend a two-step: 1) a lightweight regex + NER pre-filter we ship, 2) a customer-side redaction step for anything regulated. For the POC we can run your corpus through our pre-filter and show false positives/negatives stats.
[02:24] Priya: That would be helpful. We'll want to know the true positive rate and false positive rate for names/phones/emails.
[02:30] Avery: Ok note: Marcus will run the corpus through the filter and produce a short report.
[02:34] [00:03:00] Tomás: Moving to performance: our target is p95 sub-300 ms for single-turn customer queries at 512 token context average; throughput target is ~1200 req/min at peak. Cost target is around $0.0007 per token equivalent — is that realistic?
[03:00] Marcus: p95 < 300ms is tight but achievable on Dedicated instances with auto-batching tuned; on hosted we can approximate but may see higher variance. For throughput, 1200 req/min at average tokens 512 is roughly X tokens/sec, we typically size GPUs around those traffic profiles. For cost, depends on quantization model variant — with 8-bit quant we can approach your cost target.
[03:25] Priya: What's the benchmark we'll run? Does Redwood provide a harness?
[03:29] Marcus: Yes we'll provide a containerized harness that replays your traces at configurable concurrency, measures latency distributions (p50/p95/p99), token throughput, and also tests redaction-on-the-fly performance. We'll also measure KV cache hit rates if you enable prefix caching.
[03:45] Tomás: KV cache? Sorry I heard K V cash earlier.
[03:49] Marcus: (laughs) KV cache — key-value cache for continuations and repeated prefixes, it can lower token generation cost and latency for similar queries.
[03:54] Priya: For the POC we only need a mini-benchmark: one 4-hour run at production concurrency and one 24-hour soak at lower concurrency. Does that sound reasonable?
[04:04] Marcus: Yes, we propose Phase 1: 4-hour stress run to validate latency/throughput; Phase 2: 24-hour soak to validate stability and retention configs.
[04:12] [00:10:00] Lena: On compliance: we need an evidence pack — audit logs, SAML SSO integration, RBAC model, and proof of encryption at rest and in transit. Can Redwood provide those artifacts during the POC?
[04:24] Avery: We can provide our standard security pack (SOC2 Type II evidence), SSO integration guide, and a live demo of audit logs for the POC environment. For dedicated/private we can show KMS integration with customer-owned keys.
[04:36] Tomás: Data residency — some portion of traffic must be routed through the EU region. Can you support region pinning for the POC?
[04:44] Marcus: Yes, routing policies can pin to eu-west-1 for the POC. There is a small provisioning lead time but we can have it ready for the scheduled benchmark.
[04:52] Priya: About prompt storage: we want an option where prompts are never stored in plaintext. Either client-side redaction, or server-side redaction where only a redacted prompt is persisted. Which options are available?
[05:03] Marcus: Three modes: 1) Client-side redaction — customer removes PII before sending; 2) Server-side immediate redaction — incoming prompt is parsed, PII masked and only redacted prompt used/stored; 3) No-persist mode — no prompt stored beyond ephemeral memory used for the call, logs only send hashes/metadata. For POC we can test modes 2 and 3.
[05:18] Tomás: Mode 2 is preferred to keep semantics for prompts but hide PII. How destructive is the redaction — do you remove or replace with [REDACTED]?
[05:25] Marcus: We replace with tags like <NAME_REDACTED>, or optionally with consistent pseudonyms for context continuity. We can show both in the report.
[05:33] Priya: Ok. For the metrics — you mentioned token-level cost and latency breakdown; do we get token-level billing for the POC?
[05:41] Avery: We can provide token-level telemetry via the console and export token-level CSVs for the POC so you can map cost to request types.
[05:48] [00:20:00] Tomás: Let's capture success criteria explicitly so we can sign off: 1) p95 latency < 300ms for typical 512-token requests under target concurrency; 2) 99.9% of prompts redacted successfully (per agreed regex/NER baseline); 3) zero plaintext prompt persistence in no-persist mode; 4) ability to decrypt audit logs with our KMS in dedicated run.
[06:10] Marcus: I will capture those as the POC success criteria. For the 99.9% redaction we should define the test set and acceptance thresholds per category (emails, SSNs, phones, names).
[06:20] Priya: We'll provide labeled examples for evaluation.
[06:24] Avery: Timeline proposal: week 1 — onboarding + harness + initial 4-hour benchmark; week 2 — remediation of redaction false positives + 24-hour soak; week 3 — final runs + evidence pack and board-ready summary. That gives you wrap by 3/20 if we start next week.
[06:40] Tomás: That matches our internal cadence. Any blockers on provisioning?
[06:44] Marcus: Only the EU region provisioning if you require dedicated capacity there — a 3–5 day lead in the worst case. If you accept hosted-no-persist in eu region we can usually provision faster.
[06:55] Lena: For audit trails we need immutable logs; can logs be forwarded to our SIEM during POC?
[07:01] Avery: Yes we can stream audit logs to your S3 or to a syslog/ Splunk endpoint; we also retain an internal immutable log for the POC envelope.
[07:09] [00:30:00] Priya: About developer experience — our engineers will need an SDK and example wiring for redaction hooks. How opinionated is Redwood on the integration?
[07:19] Marcus: We provide SDKs in Python/Node and example middleware for pre/post hooks. The pre-hook can run the NER filter. We can also accept a packaged lambda/sidecar if you prefer client-side redaction.
[07:31] Priya: Great. Marcus, can you share the sample middleware today?
[07:33] Marcus: I'll drop it in the shared folder after the call.
[07:36] Tomás: On the benchmarks, what metrics do we capture beyond latency? P95 token generation time, GPU utilization, cold-starts, retry rates?
[07:45] Marcus: We'll capture p50/p95/p99 latency, token throughput, GPU utilization, batch sizes, cold-start percentage, and error rates. We'll also track redaction CPU overhead separately.
[07:55] Priya: Will the redaction step add a lot of latency?
[07:58] Marcus: It depends; the regex pre-filter is negligible (<5–15ms), the NER pass can add 30–100ms depending on model. We can run it asynchronously or inline. For tight p95 targets we recommend server-side lightweight regex + hashed tokenization inline, and run a deeper NER in a parallel pipeline for logging/QA.
[08:20] Lara (note: misattributed as Lora by auto-transcript): Sorry, that's Lena, not Lara.
[08:23] Lena: (laughs) it's Lena.
[08:25] [00:40:00] Tomás: We also want to understand fallback behavior if Dedicated capacity saturates. Does Redwood fallback to smaller models or to hosted pool?
[08:34] Avery: Yes, smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants, either in a cheaper capacity tier or across regions. Fallback policies are configurable per-route with automatic rollbacks if latency or quality regress. We'll define that in the SOW.
[08:46] Priya: We need to keep control over fallback for regulatory reasons — so disable cross-border fallback in the EU flows.
[08:53] Marcus: We'll mark EU flows as region-pinned and disable cross-region fallback in policy.
[08:58] [00:50:00] Tomás: Anything else? Pricing for the POC — how do you quantify dedicated vs hosted?
[09:06] Avery: For the POC we can do a short-term discounted dedicated allocation + engineering support included. The SOW will list the provisional pricing bands. For hosted tests we'll charge by token use and a small infra fee for the benchmarking harness.
[09:17] Priya: Please include an upper bound on cost so procurement can approve the spend.
[09:21] Avery: We'll include not-to-exceed numbers in the SOW.
[09:24] Marcus: For the mini-benchmark we recommend a scoped data size so costs stay predictable: e.g., 100k total tokens for the 4-hour run and 1M tokens for the soak.
[09:34] Tomás: Sounds reasonable.
[09:36] Avery: Ok recap of agreed items: (1) success criteria as Tomás listed; (2) Redwood to provide harness, middleware, and pre-filter results; (3) BlueHarbor to provide anonymized prompt corpus and compliance list; (4) SOW and pricing to be delivered by 3/4; (5) follow-up benchmark run scheduled 3/10.
[09:56] Priya: Confirmed.
[09:58] Lena: Confirmed.
[10:00] Avery: Great, thanks everyone. We'll send the SOW and drop the harness link. Talk soon.
